extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, researchers, policymakers and activists interested in blasphemy laws and freedom of expression
extracted.subtask_description: Comparative overview and evaluation of blasphemy laws, related penal provisions, international human-rights standards, enforcement patterns, and campaigns for repeal across multiple jurisdictions. The page surveys statutes, case examples, and international guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: ICCPR Article 19 & Article 20 restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 19 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights obliges signatory countries to guarantee freedom of expression; paragraph 3 allows certain restrictions necessary and provided by law to safeguard reputations, national security, public order, or public health or morals. Article 20 obliges countries to prohibit 'propaganda for war or advocacy of national, racial or religious hatred that constitutes incitement to discrimination, hostility or violence.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These articles set the international boundary for permissible restrictions on speech: states may limit expression only when the restriction falls within Article 19(3)'s narrow grounds, and must prohibit only forms of advocacy that amount to incitement under Article 20. Use Article 19/20 to evaluate whether domestic blasphemy restrictions are lawful under ICCPR.

rubrics_metrics.name: UN Human Rights Committee General Comment No. 34 (para 48)
rubrics_metrics.description: Paragraph 48: 'Prohibitions of displays of lack of respect for a religion or other belief system, including blasphemy laws, are incompatible with the Covenant, except in the specific circumstances envisaged in article 20, paragraph 2... Such prohibitions must also comply with the strict requirements of article 19, paragraph 3... Nor would it be permissible for such prohibitions to be used to prevent or punish criticism of religious leaders or commentary on religious doctrine and tenets of faith.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General Comment 34 interprets ICCPR to mean blasphemy laws are generally incompatible with freedom of expression except where speech crosses into Article 20(2) incitement. It warns against discriminatory application and use to censor legitimate religious critique; use it as an authoritative interpretive standard when assessing blasphemy laws' human-rights compatibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rabat Plan of Action recommendation (2012)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Rabat Plan of Action concluded that 'At the national level, blasphemy laws are counter-productive... many of these blasphemy laws afford different levels of protection to different religions and have often proved to be applied in a discriminatory manner... the right to freedom of religion or belief... does not include the right to have a religion or a belief that is free from criticism or ridicule.' It recommended that 'States that have blasphemy laws should repeal these as such laws have a stifling impact on the enjoyment of freedom of religion or belief and healthy dialogue and debate about religion.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat repeal as a recommended state practice when laws are overbroad or applied discriminatorily; the Plan is an expert-policy document supporting abolition and highlighting harms (stifling debate, discrimination).

rubrics_metrics.name: Council of Europe Recommendation 1805 (2007)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe adopted a resolution that 'blasphemy should not be a criminal offence' and Recommendation 1805 set guidelines for member states in view of Articles 10 (freedom of expression) and 9 (freedom of thought, conscience and religion) of the European Convention on Human Rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For European jurisdictions, Recommendation 1805 functions as soft-law guidance advising against criminalisation of blasphemy and encouraging protection of free expression consistent with ECHR jurisprudence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discriminatory application as a central evaluative criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Many blasphemy laws 'afford different levels of protection to different religions and have often proved to be applied in a discriminatory manner.' Such discriminatory enforcement has led to persecution of religious minorities, dissenters, atheists and non-theists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing a blasphemy law or prosecution, examine whether the law is neutrally worded and evenly enforced across religions/belief systems; discriminatory patterns weaken any legitimacy and violate non‑discrimination norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose and standard in Section 295A (Indian Penal Code)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 295A (introduced 1927) criminalises 'hate speech that insults or attempts to insult the religion or the religious beliefs' of any class of citizen 'with deliberate and malicious intention to outrage their religious feelings.' An important difference from English common law is that the defendant must have this 'deliberate and malicious intention.' The section was described as intended to maintain 'public order in a multireligious and religiously sensitive society.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate prosecutions under 295A by scrutinising mens rea (deliberate and malicious intention) and whether invocation of the section legitimately aimed at public order or was used to silence debate. The page notes 295A has been used to stifle honest discussion and there have been calls for repeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Myanmar Penal Code: Chapter XV offences relating to religion (sections 295–298)
rubrics_metrics.description: Offences listed: 295. Injuring or defiling place of worship, with intent to insult the religion of any class. 295A. Deliberate and malicious acts intended to outrage religious feelings of any class by insulting its religion or religious beliefs. 296. Disturbing religious assembly. 297. Trespassing on burial-places, etc. 298. Uttering words, etc.; with deliberate intent to wound religious feelings. Sections 295 and 295A carry a maximum penalty of two years' imprisonment, a fine, or both; sections 296–298 a maximum of one year's imprisonment, a fine, or both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the statute text and penalty ranges to assess proportionality and foreseeability. The page provides prosecution examples (VGastro bar image; Htin Lin Oo speech) showing how the provisions are applied and the severity of sentences (up to hard labour in practice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Israel Penal Code — Insult to religion (Art.170) and Injury to religious sentiment (Art.173)
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 170: 'If a person destroys, damages, or desecrates a place of worship or any object which is held sacred... with the intention of reviling their religion... liable to three years' imprisonment.' Article 173: publishing a publication or voicing words in public 'liable to crudely offend the religious faith or sentiment of others' — liable to one year's imprisonment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These provisions set actus reus and mens rea thresholds and associated penalties. The page notes the law has been rarely enforced but gives the 1997 example of a right-wing activist sentenced to two years for leaflets depicting Muhammad as a pig.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enumerated prohibited acts in specific national laws (Thailand example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Thailand's 1962 Sangha Act and the 1956 penal code outlaw insults or defamation of Buddhism and clergy; examples include damaging statues of the Buddha; stealing, buying or taking them out of Thailand; taking photos of them; sitting with feet facing them; touching them on the head; and wearing tattoos depicting the Buddha. Violations range from 1 to 7 years imprisonment, to fines of 2,000 to 14,000 baht.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating national statutes, note specific banned conduct (some culturally specific) and prescribed penalties; foreign visitors are warned to avoid these acts. Use examples to assess cultural scope and proportionality of prohibitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory mens rea distinctions (example: India vs English common law)
rubrics_metrics.description: Indian Section 295A requires a 'deliberate and malicious intention of outraging religious feelings' for conviction, whereas traditional English common law lacked that explicit mens rea requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mens rea specifications (deliberate/malicious intent) are central evaluative criteria: stricter mens rea requirements narrow criminal liability and protect legitimate criticism; their absence expands state power to prosecute speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Penalties and enforcement patterns across jurisdictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Penalties differ widely (e.g., Myanmar: up to two years; Thailand: 1–7 years and fines; Israel: up to 3 or 1 year depending on offence). Enforcement also ranges from rare prosecutions to harsh sentences and hard labour, and often differs between groups (e.g., Hui protestors let off while Uyghurs imprisoned in China).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess proportionality by comparing statutory penalties to the harm targeted, and examine real-world enforcement patterns for selective or politicised application. Examples on the page (VGastro, Htin Lin Oo, Hebron leaflet case) illustrate outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of colonial-era penal provisions as legal basis
rubrics_metrics.description: Many modern blasphemy or related offences derive from British-era laws (e.g., Section 295A introduced in 1927 in British India, Penal Code of 1860 provisions criminalising insults to religion). These provisions were often framed to 'maintain public order' in multireligious societies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical origins matter for interpreting purpose and assessing contemporary legitimacy: laws created for colonial public-order concerns may be ill-suited to modern free-expression standards and can be repurposed to suppress debate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Campaigns for repeal and comparative repeal trends as evaluative evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: A global campaign 'End Blasphemy Laws' and numerous country examples (France 1881; Sweden 1970; Norway 2009/2015; Netherlands 2014; Iceland 2015; Malta 2016; Canada 2018; New Zealand 2019; Ireland 2020; Scotland 2021; etc.) show a trend of repeal or abolition in many jurisdictions. International bodies and NGOs have advocated repeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The presence of a repeal movement and a growing list of jurisdictions that have abolished blasphemy laws can be used as normative and empirical evidence when arguing for reform or repeal in other countries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Venice Commission reporting and constitutional advisory guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: The Venice Commission issued reports about blasphemy, religious insult, and incitement to religious hatred, noting which European states still had offences and providing constitutional-level analysis and recommendations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Venice Commission analyses are authoritative for constitutional compatibility within Council of Europe states; use them to evaluate national statutes against freedom-of-expression and equality standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: State practice and media/official responses as indicators of normative approach
rubrics_metrics.description: State actions and state-run media responses (e.g., Chinese state media attacking Charlie Hebdo and advocating limiting freedom of speech after the 2015 attacks; public burnings and arrests for 'Xing Fengsu') illustrate how governments may prioritize social harmony or intercommunal peace over unfettered expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate a jurisdiction not only by statute text but by state rhetoric and media practice: official endorsement of limitations, or selective protection of some groups, indicates the practical scope and intent of blasphemy-related rules.
